newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire Premier Kengo to keep post in crisis govt - tv.
newsitem.headline: Zaire Premier Kengo to keep post in crisis govt - tv.

text.p: Zaire's squabbling political leadership moved towards agreement on a crisis government on Monday, but President Mobuto Sese Seko has yet to give it his stamp of approval.

A communique broadcast on state television on Monday night and signed by Mobutu's political movement as well as some opposition members said incumbent Prime Minister Leon Kengo wa Dondo will retain his post in a new crisis government.
Mobutu, who returned home last Tuesday after more than four months of cancer treatment in Europe, is likely to have the final word, however.
He has vowed to take on rebels led by ethnic Tutsi Zaireans who have seized territory in eastern Zaire since taking up arms in October.
He gave politicians until noon on Monday to decide on the composition of a new government to deal with the conflict.

The communique was signed well after deadline and key figures in the opposition including Etienne Tshisekedi, and the leader of a breakaway faction of his UDPS party, Frederic Kbassa Maliba, were not included.
On Monday afternoon, a heavier than normal troop presence was noticeable in Kinshasa as soldiers were moved discreetly to opposition hot-spots.
"No grounds for the prime minister to step down under article 79 of the constitution have been observed. The post of prime minister is not vacant," the communique said.

"The constitutional political families have decided in consequence to respond to the appeal by the head of state to transmit to Leon Kengo wa Dondo the conclusions of their meetings so that he can form a cris government," it added.
President Mobutu's spokesman warned at the weekend that if political leaders failed to reach an agreement the president would make the decisions himself.
"The president will make his own position known tommorrow," Professor Kabuya Lumuna, the president's spokesman, said on Monday night.
In normal circumstances Mobutu is not constitutionally empowered to nominate the prime minister and his cabinet.

Commenting on the appareent last minute consensus among political leaders to retain Kengo in place, Professor Lumuna said: "It gives him a strong chance but it should be seen simply as a stage in the process."

Other members of Mobutu's political camp were more explicit: "In principal this means that the prime minister will remain in place," Banza Mukalayi, the vice president of president Mobutu's movement, told Reuters.
But opposition figures, who have warned there will be trouble in Kinshasa if Kengo retains his post, say that the supposed consensus among some politicians is invalid.
"We have not agreed to retain Kengo. He has simply cheated public opinion with this communique," said Make Malaga, spokesman for opposition leader Frederic Kibassa.

Supporters of radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, who commands widespread popularity in the poorer neighbourhoods of Kinshasa, say they will block the capital with protest marches if their leader is not renamed prime minister.
Tshisekedi has said he is the only legitimate prime minister in Zaire ever since he was sacked from the position three years ago in favour of a Mobutu appointee.
